claims.text: The target eutectic HEA has a disordered FCC phase and an ordered B2 phase.
The initial B2 phase has low or negligible local chemical order beyond its stated B2 ordering.
Intermediate aging at approximately 650–800 K develops strong LCO within the B2 phase.
Aging in the proposed range is insufficient to cause grain coarsening or impurity segregation at boundaries.
During mechanical testing, available thermal energy is comparable to the activation barriers created by LCO.
Increasing LCO increases complex stacking-fault energy and antiphase-boundary energy.
LCO produces a spatially heterogeneous or rugged energy landscape for dislocation motion.
The rugged LCO energy landscape increases activation barriers for dislocation motion.
Dislocations in the B2 phase are forced to move through nanoscale segment detrapping rather than smooth glide.
At intermediate aging conditions, LCO strength is maximal relative to available thermal energy.
LCO-induced dislocation pinning causes the dramatic loss of ductility and brittle failure.
At higher aging temperatures, thermal activation enables dislocations to overcome LCO barriers and restores ductility.
Ductility should evolve non-monotonically from high ductility in the random state, to brittle failure at intermediate aging conditions, and back to higher ductility after higher-temperature aging.
A random solid-solution state has lower dislocation activation barriers and higher ductility than the strongly ordered intermediate state.
The embrittlement regime begins when the LCO-induced dislocation barrier exceeds kT and ends before phase decomposition or grain coarsening becomes dominant.
The NSD mechanism was previously observed in a single-phase FCC alloy.
The single-phase FCC NSD mechanism can be transferred directly to the B2 phase of a eutectic FCC/B2 alloy.
Smooth dislocation glide despite strong LCO would falsify the proposed NSD mechanism.
A correlation between brittle failure and grain-boundary segregation rather than intragranular B2 dislocation pinning would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis permits all specimens to be mechanically tested at room temperature after aging, yet attributes recovery after higher-temperature aging to greater thermal energy available for barrier crossing. If deformation occurs at the same room temperature, kT during deformation does not increase with prior aging temperature; recovery would instead require an aging-induced reduction or alteration of the barriers, which is not specified.
